cells.tense: You've got the pen right now, in the middle of the work — clear about what's in front of you and easy about saying so.
cells.ask: Take ten minutes with one thing you're tending and just watch it — no deciding what it needs, no figuring where it's headed. What it gives back is a look that comes before the next move, and you get to keep it.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day you notice what's in front of you while your hands are already on it — you water what's dry, leave alone what's fine, let a thing stay the shape it is. You don't have to work at it. Seeing and doing happen close enough together that it's easy to miss how much of the good here depends on your eyes being honest.

You don't announce it and you don't hold it back to seem modest. It comes out in the small adjustments, in what you don't touch. What you tend relaxes around that kind of attention. Looking at something clearly is how you're built to care for it, and it's feeding whatever comes next — taking ten minutes to watch without a purpose keeps it that way.

cells.tense: Your eyes are already on what hasn't happened yet — reading the next version of what you tend before it's arrived, and getting ready for it.
cells.ask: Pick something you're tending and set down every plan for it for one hour — look at it as it is today, no fixing, no forecast. It returns you to a look with nothing riding on what you find.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day you watch what you tend as it is today — you see the new leaf, you see the quiet, you see it wasn't asking for anything, and that's the whole of what you do about it. The look is close, and the closeness is why it lands.

Lately the looking has gone forward. You're checking on the thing that hasn't happened, preparing for the problem before it shows, and every ordinary glance gets spent on a version that may not arrive. The watching is still careful. It's aimed at a day that isn't here, and that aim has more hold on you than what's actually in the room. Setting the forecast down for an hour is what brings the eyes back to the thing itself.
cells.sheetLine: You're watching a future version of what you tend, and it's the one you answer to.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door already closed behind you, and what you tend has carried on past where your eyes last checked.
cells.ask: Choose one thing near you that you haven't really looked at and say one true thing about it out loud — its colour, its state, its size. It shows you what your attention does when it comes back onto something living.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day you take a fresh look at what you tend — walk past it, see it's moved, see it hasn't, and the look is what decides what you do next. Your hands follow your eyes instead of your memory of them.

At the moment the looking has gone thin. You do the caring from what you remember about the thing rather than from what's in front of you now, and the fresh look hasn't been taken. The caring isn't gone; it's running on old notes. Naming one plain true thing about something you can see is what switches the eyes back on, and once they're on, the care has something to run on.

cells.tense: You're taking in what's real here all day, and you haven't set it down anywhere as yours.
cells.ask: Say "I see that" about one plain thing in front of you today, out loud, in your own voice. What it gives back is a spot to stand where what you notice is stated rather than assumed.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day your looking is what the care is built on — you catch a change in the thing you tend before anyone else does, and your next move comes out of what you saw, not out of a rule. That's the good version, and it's mostly invisible because it's so smooth.

You're reading what's here, all day long. Catch yourself adjusting to something you noticed and you'll see the whole day has been run on it. But if someone asked, the answer would be it just worked out, or that's obvious. The looking didn't stop; calling it yours didn't happen. Saying so out loud, once, about one small thing, is what keeps the clear look from reading as somebody else's luck.
cells.sheetLine: You're already seeing what's here. Naming it as yours is the next small move.

attempts.check: The one personal claim I can't support from the record is the Too Much cell's picture of the person bracing over what they tend — checking it before it's grown instead of simply being with it. A reader might say: I don't brace, I just plan well, and I'm not sitting over anything. The ask in every cell is an experiment a camera could see — look without naming, write one line plainly, water without checking — and it teaches something about how seeing works even if my read of the status is wrong for them. The sentence in the Balanced cell that gives the most back to me as writer rather than to them is the 'steady enough to be a light without claiming anything' close; I've kept it but trimmed its self-admiring shape.
